text:
Some Target shopping baskets have a little Bluetooth tag on them. That part is true, and Snopes confirmed it. But the way it’s being shared online mixes up two separate stories, so here’s what’s real.

The basket tags send their location to Target’s smart overhead LED lights. The same system powers the in-store map in the Target app and can send you offers based on where you are in the store. Target has used this kind of technology since around 2015, and its privacy policy mentions in-store tracking with Bluetooth and LED lights. According to Snopes, the tag only sends location. It can’t tie that path to you unless you’re using the Target app with location turned on.

The pricing story is older. Back in 2019, KARE 11 in Minneapolis found that some prices in the Target app went up once shoppers walked into the store. In 2022, Target paid more than $5 million to settle a case brought by several California district attorneys. The judgment bars Target from using its app to raise an online price based solely on a shopper’s location.

So no, there’s no evidence the basket trackers are being used to raise your prices. But the bigger worry behind all of this is real. It’s called surveillance pricing, which means using your personal data to decide what you specifically pay. This year, Connecticut, Maryland and New Jersey became the first states to ban it for groceries. More states are looking at doing the same.

What you can do:
~Check the price on Target(dot)com or in the app before you get to the register. If the online price is lower, ask whether they’ll match it.
~Go into your phone settings and limit the Target app’s location access to while using the app, or turn it off.
~Use the store’s price checker scanners, and keep an eye on your receipt.

Stores are using more and more technology to figure out what we’ll pay. The best thing we can do is be just as informed.

Sources: Snopes, KARE 11, CBS News, Sonoma County District Attorney’s Office, Stateline, TechCrunch

text:
At 56, I thought the greatest love of my life was buried in the past.

Then a woman walked into my bookstore carrying a box of letters I had written to her 27 years earlier.

She placed them on the counter, looked me in the eyes, and said:

“Daniel, I think you deserve to know why I never answered the last one.”

My hands began to shake.

Because Emily Parker wasn't just my first love.

She was the woman I had planned to marry.

And the last letter I sent her was the reason I never loved anyone the same way again.

But what she told me next changed everything I believed about our past. 
Emily and I met in 1997 at a little diner in Columbus, Ohio.

I was 27, working at a printing company and saving every spare dollar to open a bookstore someday.

She was 26, a kindergarten teacher who believed every child deserved at least one adult who never gave up on them.

She came into the diner every Thursday after work.

I started coming every Thursday, too.

One evening, she caught me staring at her.

“Do you always look at people like you're trying to memorize them?” she asked.

“Only the interesting ones,” I replied.

She laughed so hard that the waitress came over to check on us.

For three years, we built a life out of ordinary things.

Cheap pizza on Friday nights. Long drives with the windows down. Christmas mornings at her parents' house. Notes tucked into each other's coat pockets.

Emily called my bookstore dream ridiculous.

Then she bought me a secondhand wooden bookcase for my birthday and wrote on a card:

For the man who will one day give a thousand stories a home.

I kept that card for 27 years.

Even after she was gone.

Especially after she was gone.
In the summer of 1999, I asked Emily to marry me.

There was no expensive restaurant or diamond big enough to make a mortgage payment.

Just a picnic beside a lake, a silver ring I had saved six months to buy, and a question I had practiced in front of my bathroom mirror.

She said yes before I finished asking.

We planned to get married the following spring.

Then I received a job offer in Cincinnati that could finally make my bookstore dream possible. Emily had also been offered a teaching position there.

We agreed to move together.

But two weeks before our wedding, Emily disappeared from my life.

She stopped answering my calls.

Her apartment was empty.

Her parents told me she had decided to move away and start over.

I wrote her a letter every week for six months.

The final one said:

Emily, if you no longer love me, tell me yourself. I can survive the truth. What I cannot survive is spending the rest of my life wondering why you left.

She never replied.

Eventually, I stopped writing.

I moved to Cincinnati alone.

Years later, I opened my bookstore.

I married someone else, but that marriage ended after seven years. Emily married, too, according to a mutual friend.

I told myself we had both moved on.

But every Thursday, I still thought about the girl who used to laugh so hard in a diner that strangers turned to look.

text:
This is the impressive spillway of the Hoover Dam, a colossal concrete tunnel designed to divert excess water from Lake Mead’s reservoir during extreme floods. 

With a vertical shaft about 15 meters wide that descends some 180 meters into the gloom of the rock, the structure connects to the old diversion tunnels excavated in the canyon during the 1930s. The narrow inspection walkway seen above offers a striking perspective on its dizzying scale.

Unlike traditional spillways on the crest of a dam, this “glory hole” system acts as a gigantic drain that prevents reservoir waters from overflowing and damaging the main dam wall. During the construction of this megastructure in the midst of the Great Depression, the excavation and concrete lining of these shafts represented one of the most dangerous and innovative civil engineering feats of its time.

Despite its capacity to discharge hundreds of thousands of cubic feet of water per second, the spillway has rarely been used throughout its history. It has only been put into operation on a few occasions, most notably during the massive floods of 1983, when the waters of the Colorado River reached record levels. 

Today, this colossal spillway stands as a silent testament to the architectural and industrial splendor of the 20th century.

Part 2 of 2. The Atlanta Georgian, Saturday, October 25, 1913, "Atlanta's Prejudice as Bitter as Russia's, Declares Attorney," continued: Reuben R. Arnold's Saturday speech to Judge L. S. Roan, as the paper printed it on Pages 2 and 8.

Appendix: Full article transcript, continued

PAGE 2, COLUMNS 1 & 7.

ARNOLD ARRAIGNS FRANK TRIAL CROWD

RUSSIAN PERSECUTION OF JEWS CALLED MORE JUST THAN FRANK CASE

Reuben R. Arnold, of counsel for Leo Frank, resumed an address ringing with denunciation of the conditions under which Frank was convicted of the murder of Mary Phagan, when the hearing on a new trial re-convened Saturday in the library of the State capitol.

He uttered a scathing arraignment of the mob spirit which he declared had overawed the jurors and made impossible any other than that of guilty.

No victim of persecution in Russia, he asserted, ever had suffered more unjustly than Leo Frank.

The attorney drew a dramatic comparison of the Frank trial with that of Mendel Beiliss, the Russian Jew, whose trial in Kiev on the charge of "ritual murder" has aroused the civilized world.

As outrageous and horribly unjust as everyone concedes the charges against Beiliss, Arnold maintained they are surpassed in this respect by the accusations on which Frank had been convicted.

Frank's attorney was to be followed by Solicitor Dorsey, representing the State.

The defense having the burden of proof, has the last argument.

Luther Z. Rosser, chief of counsel for the defense, will make this argument.

It was regarded as probable that all of the addresses would be concluded by evening, and that the fight would be in the hands of Judge Roan for decision.

Responsibility on Judge.

"It takes thirteen jurors to murder a man in cold blood in Georgia," exclaimed Arnold, addressing the court.

"The trial judge has to approve the verdict brought in by the twelve jurors. This puts a terrible responsibility onto the judge. With his superior experience and his thorough knowledge of law, he is in a much better position to weigh accurately and intelligently the evidence which has been submitted.

"A judge once said that it was up to the jury to decide whom to believe, but the Superior Court did not approve this evasion of plain duty on the part of the trial judge."

"This is a most unusual case. There have been murders before and there will be after this. The example of Cain will be followed until the end of time. You may pick up the newspapers any day and read of these crimes. They do not mitigate this murder in the least. The crime at the pencil factory was atrocious as any in the history of the State."

"But the intense feeling over this crime grows out of something else than its mere atrocity. You have got to hunt down under the surface but you have to scratch down just a little before you find that it is the same old cause that has run down through the ages."

Cites Russian Trial.

"About the only parallel in recent times is going on to-day in the holy city of Kiev, Russia, where they are trying Mendel Beiliss, a Russian Jew, for the 'ritual murder' of a 13-year-old boy. It's a case on which the civilized world looks aghast and with horror. Everyone knows that it's all a lie and a diabolical persecution. The boy was killed. There is no doubt of that. But that he was killed by Beiliss as a victim of the so-called 'ritual murder,' which, as a matter of fact, exists only in the imagination of the persecutors of the Jews, is an infamous lie, as the world knows."

"As strange as is this travesty on justice in progress in Kiev, Russia, it is no stronger than the trial which was enacted in our own city of Atlanta last August. The charges are no more ridiculous and fantastic than those brought against this young man here."

"We have had to contend against two hydraheaded propositions which confront us at every turn, prejudice and ignorance, the twin evils. We have had to contend with the spirit of the mob. This is no idle dream. It is a fact of which your honor is well aware.

Courts, Not Public, to Judge.

"The courts are organized to be experts, not the public. The public doesn't hear the whole thing thrashed out. They are not in a position to appreciate the merits of a case, no matter how much they want to do the right thing. The law is receiving a critical test right now. I've trembled more for the law than ever before. I have thought that the law has been more on trial than Leo Frank."

"We have been so circumvented and hedged about by hatred and prejudice that their influence constantly has been felt in the courtroom where a man was guaranteed a fair and impartial trial. The day when such a condition can not exist will come soon. It's here now with the enlightened citizens of the State and even somewhat with the benighted."

"We've got the best people on earth right here in this Southland. We really are the only American people. It will not be long before we are completely divested of all this prejudice, but this time, I am sorry to say, is not yet here, if one may judge by what occurred at the courthouse during the trial last August, when mobs were pushing their way into the courtroom to misbehave, when people rejoiced and smiled and threw up their caps in delight because a man was condemned to death."

"I don't believe there is another case on record that a wretch confessed to witnessing the commission of a crime against nature and lied in each of four successive affidavits on material points in his story, where his evidence would have been taken against that of a sheep-killing dog."

Conley's Evidence All.

"Yet, you would believe the infamous lies told against this man now under a sentence of death in the Tower. You would believe the charge of perversion, as base a lie as ever was heard in a courtroom. The revolting story created an impression of truth though it was the greatest strain ever put upon the credulity of a civilized and law-abiding people."

"I ask your honor: Outside the testimony of that miserable wretch, Conley, would there be any pretense of having enough evidence to convict Leo Frank? Would you do anything more than pick up your pen to grant a new trial? Would you have done anything else than discharge the jury from their box?"

"Then, what is there to constrain you to act differently than in any other case? Would anyone hesitate a minute? In an ordinary case, the inflammatory speech of Mr. Dorsey

(Continued on Page 8.)

PAGE 8, COLUMN 1.

FRANK VERDICT PERSECUTION, SAYS ARNOLD

Russian Outrages on Jews Surpassed by Atlanta Case, He Declares to Judge Roan.

Continued From Page 1.

would have disgusted the court and the spectators. The jury would have returned a verdict of not guilty without leaving their seats. Why was it different in this case?

"Have we taken leave of our senses? If so, a man was condemned to death on as flimsy a fabrication as ever was devised. No man in darkest Russia ever suffered more unjustly. I would not have believed it.

Lies From Beginning.

"Lies were circulated from the first. It is not pleasant to admit it, but falsehood travels faster than truth. People like to believe the unusual, the strange, the revolting. Lies were sworn to that make me shudder. But the prince of all the liars was Conley. If that black wretch had any conscience he some day would confess. But there's no wolf, no bear, no hyena as devoid of conscience as that 'nigger.' A man never had a better opportunity than was given him to shift the crime he had committed onto the shoulders of another. All he had to do was to answer the leading questions that were fired at him by the detectives. Why, Detective Scott testified that they even went so far as to point out the weak points in his weird tale and he forthwith patched them up.

"He made one affidavit. Then he made another, another and still another, each one differing from the one that preceded. There were the four affidavits and then came the seven interviews with the Solicitor to which the negro admitted on the stand. And when he came to testify, his story no more compared with that fourth affidavit, his final, true, unalterable statement, than anything in the world.

"Is your honor going to believe that monstrous fake, or will you say that it, at least, is so incredible that you will not forever pass on it by affirming the verdict, but, instead, will grant a new trial?"

"At the outset nothing was found against Frank. Nothing would have been found against him had he not voluntarily offered the information that he was in the factory at 12 o'clock and that Mary Phagan came in to get her pay from him.

"It was not until many days after that the State's own witness admitted that he was there, and many others had the opportunity to be in the factory at the time without the knowledge of anyone else. The detectives had a few facts that amounted to nothing. Instead of using the facts to corroborate or disprove Conley's story, they fixed up his story to fit the facts.

"The most remarkable story that the negro told came at the last as a climax. In none of the four affidavits had Conley said anything about the purse of Mary Phagan. To reporters and others he had denied ever seeing it. He was on the stand for hours under the direct examination of Solicitor Dorsey and never mentioned it. He was under the cross-examination of Mr. Rosser two days and there never was a hint that he had seen it.

"Finally, when Mr. Dorsey had him on the redirect, he said: 'Well, what about the purse, Jim?' and Jim said: 'Oh, yes, I seen it laying on Mr. Frank's desk and he taken it and put it in the safe.'

Says He DID Break Conley Down.

"Some people have said: 'Why didn't you break Conley down?' The ignorance of some persons is astounding. They think that in order to break a witness down you have to make him collapse on the stand. They think that in order to discredit a witness you have to knock him down from the witness chair as you would with an ax, but if any intelligent person will look at the mass of conflicting statements made by Conley, his palpable lies and his instant loss when he was asked about anything in which he had not been drilled, they will see whether or not he was broken down. If there is a lame place in the jury system it is in the gullibility of the ordinary run of human beings; it is in the ease with which a jury may be hoodwinked and the ease with which a fraud may be put over on them.

"So plastered over with lies and contradictions was the negro that it is monstrous to say that he was not discredited. Had he not been taken away from the jail to the police station, where he was drilled in his fantastic tale, his fabrications would have been still more apparent.

Scores Prosecutor Dorsey.

"If Leo Frank is hanged, I had rather be Leo Frank dead and in my grave than to be in the place of Hugh Dorsey who sent him there. It is certain that he led the jury off the track, blinded their eyes with prejudice and the innuendo and accusation of every crime on the calendar. Up to the murder never a charge had been made against the defendant. The evidence rose up out of the miasma of prejudice and came to confront us hydraheaded throughout the trial.

"When I think of the thirst for blood, the joy that fills people's hearts to see some man swing from the gibbet, I feel ashamed for this part of the human race. When man gets worked up into a frenzy of hatred, he is the most venomous animal in the world."

Attorney Arnold was interrupted in his address by the closing of the hearing. Before he concluded he charged that the controversy between Attorney Thomas B. Felder and Chief of Detectives Lanford had more to do with the stirring up of prejudice against Frank than any other single incident during the investigation.

The Atlanta Journal: Atlanta Police Sergeant Robert J. Brown Testifies at the Mary Phagan Coroner's Inquest, April 30, 1913

The Atlanta Journal's Report, Sergeant Dobbs's Testimony, and What the Jury Heard at Leo Frank's Murder Trial

On Wednesday, April 30, 1913, Atlanta Police Sergeant Robert J. Brown testified at the coroner's inquest into the murder of 13-year-old Mary Phagan, whose body had been discovered three days earlier in the basement of the National Pencil Company on South Forsyth Street in Atlanta, Georgia.

Brown was one of the first police officers to enter the basement after night watchman Newt Lee reported finding her body shortly after 3 o'clock on Sunday morning, April 27, 1913.

The Atlanta Journal published Brown's testimony that afternoon under the heading "Sergeant Brown Testifies," as part of its larger front-page article, "Negro Watchman Tells Story of Finding Girl's Body and Questions Fail to Shake Him." The article began on page 1, column 4, and concentrated on Brown's doubts about Lee, particularly whether he could have seen the girl's body from approximately 25 feet away with a dim lantern (AJ, 1).

The accompanying video recreates these events, showing Sergeant Brown in his Atlanta police uniform, with brief scenes of him seated at a desk. Most of the video is narrated through a portrayal of Clark Howell (1863–1936), editor of The Atlanta Constitution. The video identifies Howell by name and draws from the Constitution's May 1, 1913 coverage. However, this write-up gives the highest priority to the Atlanta Journal's April 30 reporting.

Robert J. Brown: The Atlanta Police Sergeant

Atlanta city directories help establish Sergeant Brown's identity. The 1912 directory lists Robert J. Brown as a police sergeant living at 52 Stonewall Street with Mollie Brown, apparently his wife. The 1914 directory again identifies Robert J. Brown as a police sergeant, this time residing at 56 Brookline Street. These entries strongly suggest that Robert J. Brown was the same Sergeant R. J. Brown who testified at the coroner's inquest. His full middle name, birth date, and death date remain unconfirmed (Atlanta City Directory, 6; Atlanta City Directory, 7).

Georgia State University's Atlanta Journal-Constitution Photographic Archive also preserves a photograph identified as Atlanta police officer R. J. Brown, dating to approximately 1905. The photograph carries identification number AJCR576-001c and was later used in a September 11, 1957 newspaper feature. The archive does not specifically connect the photographed officer to the Mary Phagan investigation, so that identification still needs further confirmation (GSU, 8).

Sunday, April 27, 1913: Police Enter the Pencil Factory

Shortly after 3 o'clock Sunday morning, Newt Lee telephoned Atlanta police headquarters and reported finding a dead girl in the basement of the National Pencil Company.

Call Officer W. F. Anderson received the report. Anderson, Sergeant Brown, Sergeant L. S. Dobbs, and former county policeman W. W. Rogers, known as "Boots" Rogers, drove to the factory in Rogers' automobile.

Lee admitted the officers and led them toward an opening in the floor near the elevator. They climbed down a ladder into the basement and followed him toward the rear of the building.

Brown testified that he and Dobbs were near the front of the group, striking matches while Lee carried an ordinary lantern with a dirty glass globe. The basement was dark, and the lantern gave off very little light.

The officers found Mary Phagan lying face down with her arms folded underneath her. Brown turned her over and found that her body was cold and stiff. Her face was covered with dirt and debris, and her clothing had been disturbed (AG, 2).

According to the Journal, Brown exclaimed:

"This is nothing but a child!"

The officers had been called to investigate a murder and discovered that the victim was a young girl (AJ, 1).

April 30, 1913: Brown Questions Newt Lee's Story

The Journal gave considerable attention to Brown's doubts about Lee's claim that he had discovered the body from approximately 25 feet away.

Lee had told police that the dead person was a white female. Brown questioned how he could have known that with such a weak lantern.

According to Brown, the officers could barely see the body until they were within a few feet of it. Even then, they had difficulty determining whether she was white or Black because her face was covered with dirt.

The Journal reported that Brown tried cleaning her face with shavings from the basement floor. When that did not settle the question, he pulled down her right stocking and examined the skin of her knee.

Only then, according to the Journal, could the officers be certain that the victim was white (AJ, 1).

This raised a question. If several officers had trouble identifying the girl while standing over her, how could Lee identify her from 25 feet away?

Lee offered an explanation. He said he recognized the victim's race from her hair. The Constitution's May 1 report acknowledged that this answered part of the officers' objection (AC, 3).

Brown's testimony raised doubts about Lee's account, but it did not prove that Lee was lying or involved in the murder.

Brown Describes the Body, Neck Bindings, and Basement

Brown told the jury that a cord was tied tightly around Mary Phagan's neck. He also described a strip of cloth, apparently torn from her underskirt, that had been tied around her neck.

Brown believed the cloth had been tied before the cord. He gave strangulation as his opinion of the cause of death.

He also described dirt inside the victim's mouth, injuries to her face and head, and an impression in the basement floor that looked as though something had been dragged across it. However, he could not say for certain what had caused the mark.

At the rear of the basement, Brown found a door with its locking staple pulled loose. He believed the staple had been removed from inside the building (AJ, 1; AG, 2).

Brown also described the officers' unsuccessful attempts to reach Leo M. Frank, superintendent of the National Pencil Company. Officer Anderson tried calling Frank after the discovery, telling the telephone operator that a murder had occurred and that the call was urgent. There was no answer at that early hour.

Brown explained that he remained with Lee while Anderson made the calls. He could confirm that Frank had not been reached, but not why the calls went unanswered (AG, 2).

Sergeant L. S. Dobbs Testifies at the Coroner's Inquest

Sergeant Dobbs, who entered the basement with Brown, also testified on April 30.

The Journal reported that Dobbs found two notes near Mary Phagan's body, one written on yellow paper and another on rough scratch-pad paper. He placed the body approximately 150 feet from the elevator shaft and described her hat and missing shoe lying on a trash pile.

Dobbs believed that marks on the basement floor might show where the body had been dragged. He also testified that he could barely see the victim until he was three or four feet away, supporting Brown's account of the poor lighting (AJ, 1).

Dobbs told the jury that he confronted Lee after examining the body and reading the notes, accusing him of either committing the crime or knowing who had done it.

Lee denied any involvement.

When Dobbs read part of one note referring to the night watchman, Lee reportedly responded:

"That means me."

Dobbs said Lee then identified the reference as meaning the night watchman. Investigators were trying to determine who wrote the notes and whether they were genuine or had been placed near the body to mislead police (AJ, 1).

Dobbs Tests the Visibility in the Basement

Dobbs also described an experiment conducted after daylight.

He returned to the basement and had another officer lie on the floor where Mary Phagan had been found. Dobbs then stood near the position Lee claimed to have occupied when he discovered the body.

According to the Journal, Dobbs said he could barely make out the officer unless he looked directly toward him, even in daylight.

This appeared to support Brown's doubts about whether Lee could have seen the body with his lantern in the darkness (AJ, 1).

However, Dobbs later described another experiment at Leo Frank's murder trial, and his testimony gave a somewhat different picture of what could be seen.

Was Mary Phagan Found Face Up or Face Down?

Another disagreement concerned the position of Mary Phagan's body.

Lee said he discovered her lying face up, with her head toward the rear of the building. Brown and Dobbs said they found her face down, with her head toward Forsyth Street.

The Journal gave considerable attention to this difference because it suggested that someone might have moved the body after Lee first discovered it.

Lee insisted he had not moved her.

If both accounts were accurate, someone else would have had to turn the body over before the police arrived. Another possibility was that one of the witnesses was mistaken.

The reports did not settle the question (AJ, 1; AC, 3).

July 29, 1913: Dobbs Testifies at Leo Frank's Murder Trial

Nearly three months later, Sergeant Dobbs testified for the prosecution at Leo Frank's murder trial.

Sergeant Brown does not appear among the sworn witnesses in the surviving trial Brief of Evidence.

Dobbs repeated his account of the police being called to the factory, entering the basement, and finding Mary Phagan lying face downward.

He also described the difficulty the officers had identifying the victim because of the dirt covering her face.

Dobbs said the officers cleaned her face with paper and that he personally lifted her clothing to examine the skin of her knee (Trial Brief, 4).

This differed from the April 30 Journal report, which credited Brown with pulling down the stocking. The Georgian had attributed that action to Officer Anderson.

The officers agreed that examining the victim's skin helped them determine her race, but the reports disagreed over who actually performed the examination.

The Nighttime Lantern Experiment

At the murder trial, Dobbs described another experiment the officers made in the basement.

They returned at night and placed a bundle approximately the size of a human body near where Mary Phagan had been found. Using a lantern, they tried to see the bundle from Lee's reported position.

Dobbs testified that the bulk of the bundle could be seen if someone looked carefully in that direction (Trial Brief, 4).

The Constitution's July 30 report also described the nighttime experiment. Dobbs said the officers used a lantern similar to Lee's and were able to see the bundle from where Lee had been standing (AC, 5).

This was different from the impression readers might have received from the Journal's April 30 coverage, which suggested Lee could hardly have seen anything.

The later experiment showed that something about the size of a body could be seen under certain conditions. That did not prove Lee could identify the victim's race from that distance, but it did weaken the suggestion that seeing anything was impossible.

Dobbs acknowledged that Lee might have seen the feet and general shape of the body without being able to identify the person.

Lee's own testimony also explained that he moved closer after first noticing something on the basement floor (Trial Brief, 4).

Dobbs Tells the Trial Jury What Brown Did

The Atlanta Constitution's July 30 report preserved an exchange between defense attorney Luther Z. Rosser and Sergeant Dobbs.

Rosser asked who cleaned Mary Phagan's face.

Dobbs answered:

"Sergeant Brown, I believe."

Rosser then asked how Brown had cleaned her face.

Dobbs replied:

"With a piece of paper."

This placed Brown's actions before the trial jury, even though Brown himself was not called to testify (AC, 5).

It also differed from the Journal's April 30 report, which said Brown used shavings. The Georgian had reported that he used paper, agreeing with Dobbs's later account.

Dobbs also testified about the drag marks, the rear basement door, and whether someone could have carried the body down the ladder.

He believed the marks suggested dragging but admitted he could not be certain what caused them. He also acknowledged that he did not know exactly how the rear door's staple had been removed.

When questioned about the ladder, Dobbs said carrying a body through the opening would have been very difficult, although he admitted a body might have been dropped through headfirst (AC, 5).

Comparing the Atlanta Journal, Georgian, and Constitution

The Atlanta Journal, April 30, 1913

The Journal concentrated on Brown's suspicions about Newt Lee, including the dirty lantern, poor lighting, and difficulty identifying the victim.

It also reported Dobbs's account of the notes, possible drag marks, rear door, and daylight experiment. The Journal's coverage presented Lee's account as having serious problems (AJ, 1).

The Atlanta Georgian, April 30, 1913

The Georgian published a longer question-and-answer account of Brown's testimony.

When asked whether Lee could have seen the body from his reported position, Brown answered:

"I can't say, but to do that one would have to look right close."

Brown also acknowledged that a partition might have hidden the girl's head and shoulders while leaving her legs visible (AG, 2).

His answer was more cautious than the Journal's summary suggested.

The Atlanta Constitution, May 1 and July 30, 1913

The Constitution's May 1 article discussed Brown's doubts but also reported Lee's explanation about recognizing the victim from her hair.

Its July 30 coverage added Dobbs's trial testimony, including the nighttime lantern experiment and the questions about Brown cleaning the victim's face (AC, 3; AC, 5).

The newspapers also disagreed over three smaller details: who examined the victim's stocking, whether Brown cleaned her face with paper or shavings, and whether the cloth or cord was tied around her neck first. The Journal said Brown believed the cloth was tied first, while the Georgian reported Brown saying the cord was tied first (AJ, 1; AG, 2; Trial Brief, 4).

These differences should be preserved as originally reported, rather than changing one newspaper's account to agree with another.

James Richard Gray: Editor of The Atlanta Journal

The Atlanta Journal was under the leadership of James Richard Gray (1859–1917) when Brown testified.

Gray was born in Adairsville, Georgia, on September 30, 1859. He attended North Georgia Agricultural College in Dahlonega and entered the legal profession in 1879.

In September 1900, Gray became editor and general manager of the Journal. By 1905, he had purchased a controlling interest and became its president.

Under Gray, the Journal expanded its sports coverage in 1901, introduced a Sunday edition in 1902, and launched a Sunday magazine in 1912.

By 1913, the newspaper was competing with the Atlanta Constitution and Atlanta Georgian for readers following the Mary Phagan investigation.

Gray remained with the Journal until his death on June 25, 1917, at age 57 (Editor & Publisher, 9; Perry, 11).

The April 30 article appeared under Gray's leadership, although no verified byline establishes that he personally wrote it.

Clark Howell: The Constitution Editor Portrayed in the Video

Most of the accompanying video is narrated through a portrayal of Clark Howell (1863–1936), editor of The Atlanta Constitution.

Howell was born in Erwinton, South Carolina, on September 21, 1863. His father, Evan P. Howell, was also closely associated with the Constitution.

After graduating from the University of Georgia in 1883, Clark worked briefly for newspapers in New York and Philadelphia before joining the Constitution in 1884.

He later became managing editor and succeeded his father as editor-in-chief in 1897. Howell also served in the Georgia legislature and remained active in state politics.

He continued his newspaper career until his death in 1936 (Eberhard, 10).

The video shows Howell in a recreated newspaper office, narrating the investigation, with shorter scenes of Sergeant Brown. These are modern recreations, not original recordings from 1913.

Did Sergeant Brown Testify at the Murder Trial or Afterward?

Brown's April 30 testimony at the coroner's inquest is documented in the Atlanta newspapers.

However, I have not found his name among the sworn witnesses in the surviving Brief of Evidence from Leo Frank's July and August 1913 murder trial.

Sergeant Dobbs testified instead, bringing several of Brown's observations before the jury. Brown was specifically mentioned when Dobbs was questioned about who cleaned Mary Phagan's face (Trial Brief, 4; AC, 5).

I have also not found a verified record of Brown giving sworn testimony or submitting an affidavit during Frank's later post-trial proceedings.

His confirmed testimony remains the April 30 coroner's inquest.

Brown and Dobbs: From the Coroner's Inquest to the Murder Trial

Brown and Dobbs were among the first officers to enter the pencil factory basement after Mary Phagan's body was discovered.

Both described the darkness, the position of the body, the bindings around her neck, and possible marks showing that something had been dragged across the floor.

Their early testimony raised questions about Newt Lee, particularly whether he could have seen and identified the girl from the position he described.

But Dobbs's later trial testimony showed that officers could see the general shape of a body-sized object during a nighttime experiment.

The newspapers also disagreed about several details of the investigation, including who examined the victim's stocking and what was used to clean her face.

Brown did not testify at the murder trial, as far as the surviving records show, but Dobbs did. His testimony gave the jury another account of the same events and allowed the defense to question what the officers had actually observed.

The April 30 Atlanta Journal report gives us Brown's suspicions during the first days of the investigation. The Georgian's longer account, the Constitution's coverage, and Dobbs's trial testimony help us compare those early statements with what was later presented in court.

Together, these records give us a clearer picture of what the Atlanta police found inside the National Pencil Company basement on April 27, 1913, and what they could and could not establish from the evidence.

Sergeant R. J. Brown Tells His Story of Finding Mary Phagan’s Body

The Atlanta Georgian, Wednesday, April 30, 1913

Coroner’s Inquest, Atlanta, Fulton County, Georgia

Saturday, April 26, 1913: Mary Phagan’s Last Visit to the Factory

On Saturday, April 26, 1913, thirteen-year-old Mary Phagan went to the National Pencil Company at 37–41 South Forsyth Street in downtown Atlanta to collect her wages. It was Confederate Memorial Day, a Georgia holiday, and the factory was largely closed. Leo M. Frank, the factory superintendent, acknowledged that Mary entered his second-floor office to collect $1.20 in wages. In his statement to investigators on Monday, April 28, Frank placed her visit between 12:05 and 12:10 p.m., possibly around 12:07. He maintained that she received her money and left. She was never seen alive again by any witness whose identification was established beyond dispute (BOE, 1).

That visit placed Frank among the last people known to have seen Mary alive. It also made his account of her departure important to the investigation. Detectives needed to determine whether Mary left the building, where she was attacked, how her body reached the basement, and who had access to the factory during the hours after she disappeared.

Sunday, April 27, 1913: Newt Lee Discovers the Body

During the early morning hours of Sunday, April 27, night watchman Newt Lee discovered a body in the factory basement. Lee said he had gone downstairs to use the basement toilet while making his rounds. As he left the toilet, he noticed something lying near a partition. At first he thought someone had placed an object there to frighten him. When he went closer, he realized it was a body.

Lee telephoned Atlanta police headquarters and reported his discovery. Contemporary witnesses gave somewhat different times for the call and the officers' arrival, generally placing the first response shortly after 3 a.m. Sergeant R. J. Brown was among the officers dispatched to investigate. The Atlanta Georgian subsequently identified Brown as the officer in charge of the morning watch (AG, 2).

Sunday, April 27, 1913: Sergeant Brown Responds to the Factory

Brown told the coroner’s jury that Call Officer Anderson answered Lee’s telephone report. Anderson, Sergeant L. S. Dobbs, Brown, and W. W. “Boots” Rogers traveled to the factory in Rogers’s automobile. When they reached the building, the entrance was locked. The officers shook the door until Lee appeared and admitted them.

The police asked Lee where the body was located. Lee directed them toward an opening in the floor near the elevator. The officers descended a ladder through this opening, known as a scuttle hole, into the basement. Brown said he and Dobbs were near the front of the group, striking matches and looking around. Lee carried an ordinary lantern whose glass globe was dirty. Its light was weak, making the basement difficult to examine (AG, 2).

The officers were entering a long basement filled with factory refuse, shavings, dirt, and stored materials. A boiler stood along one side, a toilet was farther back, and a partition partly concealed the area where Mary lay. Sergeant Dobbs later estimated that the body was approximately 150 feet from the elevator shaft. Brown estimated the distance between the basement toilet and the body at approximately 25 feet (AG, 2; AG, 3).

Sunday, April 27, 1913: Brown Examines Mary Phagan’s Body

Brown described finding the body lying face downward, with both arms folded underneath it. He was struck by how young the victim appeared. According to the Georgian, he exclaimed, “For Heavens' sake; It is only a child.”

Brown said he turned the body over and found it cold and stiff. Her face was covered with dirt, trash, and cinders. The officers initially had difficulty determining whether the victim was White or Black. Brown used a piece of paper to wipe material from her face, and Officer Anderson pulled down a stocking to examine the skin of her leg. They then recognized that the victim was White (AG, 2).

The condition of the body was important for two reasons. First, Brown was describing physical evidence he personally observed within a relatively short time of the discovery. Second, the heavy dirt and the position of the body raised questions about whether Mary had been killed where she lay or moved there after the attack.

The coldness and stiffness of the body were also observations worth recording. They were consistent with death having occurred before the officers arrived, although Brown could not determine the precise hour of death from those conditions alone.

Sunday, April 27, 1913: Dirt Inside the Mouth and Injuries to the Face

Brown described Mary's mouth as open, with dirt on her lips, around the corners, and inside her mouth. He estimated that her tongue protruded approximately one and one-half inches. He also reported blood at her ears and mouth and described a bubbly streak extending from her nostrils.

The coroner asked whether the dirt inside her mouth could have resulted from the body lying face downward. Brown answered, “Not all of it.” This was an important answer because he believed at least some of the dirt could not be explained simply by her final position on the basement floor (AG, 2).

For investigators, the dirt raised questions about how Mary had been handled and whether her face had been pressed against a dirty surface during the attack or afterward. It was possible that some of this material had entered her mouth before the body was placed where the officers found it. Brown’s observation, however, did not establish precisely when the dirt entered her mouth or who was responsible.

Sunday, April 27, 1913: The Cord and Torn Underskirt Around Mary’s Neck

Brown found two separate bindings around Mary Phagan’s neck. One was a cord, and the other was made from two strips torn from her underskirt and tied together. He described the cord as looped around the neck, with a draw knot. He believed it had been pulled tight enough to strangle her.

When asked what caused Mary's death, Brown answered, “Strangulation.” He also said he believed the cord had been applied before the underskirt strips (AG, 2).

These observations provided early evidence of deliberate violence. The bindings were physical objects that investigators could examine, compare, and later introduce in connection with medical testimony. The torn underskirt also showed that material from Mary's own clothing had been used at some point during the attack or the handling of her body.

An important discrepancy appears in the April 30 newspaper accounts. The Atlanta Journal reported Brown as believing that the underskirt band had been tied around the neck before the rope. The Atlanta Georgian reported the opposite. Both newspapers described the presence of the bindings, but their accounts differed on the order in which Brown thought they were applied. That difference should be preserved when quoting his testimony (AJ, 4).

Sunday, April 27, 1913: The Unfastened Stocking Supporter

Dr. J. W. Hurt, the Fulton County physician, questioned Brown about Mary's clothing below the shoulders, particularly the stocking that Officer Anderson had pulled down during the examination.

Brown said that the stocking supporter was already loose. He did not believe its catch had been broken. He also said Anderson had not loosened the fastening or used force while examining the body.

These answers helped establish that the supporter was unfastened before the officers inspected the leg, according to Brown's recollection. This detail deserved attention because investigators were examining possible evidence of a sexual attack and the disturbed condition of Mary's clothing. An unfastened supporter by itself could not establish that an assault had occurred, but it formed part of the early record of the condition in which her clothing was found (AG, 2).

Sunday, April 27, 1913: Possible Dragging Marks Across the Basement

One of Brown’s important observations concerned the ground between the basement entrance and the place where Mary's body was discovered. He reported seeing an impression along the pathway that looked as though something had been dragged.

Brown was careful about the limits of this observation. The basement was poorly illuminated, and he said it was difficult to determine exactly what had produced the impression.

Sergeant Dobbs gave stronger testimony about dragging marks. He said that when officers returned to the area after daylight, they could trace signs of dragging from the elevator area toward the location of the body. He described the marks as continuous and placed a missing shoe near the apparent path (AG, 2; AG, 3).

For the eventual prosecution of Frank, this was important circumstantial evidence. If Mary had been attacked on an upper floor and brought down by elevator, the killer or an accomplice would still have had to move her from the elevator area to the rear basement. A continuous dragging trail would fit that possibility.

It did not prove where the original attack occurred. There were several possible explanations for movement in the basement, and Brown himself could not positively identify the impression as a mark made by Mary's body. His contribution was an early observation that supported further examination of the route.

Sunday, April 27, 1913: The Rear Basement Door and Its Pulled Staple

Brown also examined the rear basement door, a possible exit from the building. He told the coroner’s jury that the staple and lock had been unfastened. Although the door was closed, it was unlocked, and the staple had been pulled.

When asked whether the staple could have been pulled from outside, Brown answered that it could not (AG, 2).

This observation raised another question for investigators. If Brown was correct about the fastening, someone may have manipulated the rear door from inside the factory. That created the possibility of a person entering the basement through another part of the building and later leaving through the rear.

The unfastened door could fit a theory that the murderer had used the basement as an escape route. It could also support a defense argument that the building was not completely secure and that someone other than Frank might have had access. Brown did not identify the person who pulled the staple, when it was pulled, or whether the killer used that door.

The important fact was the condition of the door as Brown found it, which investigators could compare with later testimony about access to the factory.

Sunday, April 27, 1913: The Two Handwritten Notes

Brown told the coroner that two handwritten notes were recovered near Mary's body. He thought that Sergeant Dobbs had picked up one and that he himself had picked up the other. Dobbs also identified the notes during his own testimony.

The papers became a central part of the investigation because they appeared to describe the crime and referred to a Black man and the night watchman. Investigators initially examined whether Lee had written them. The unusual wording and the apparent attempt to direct blame raised questions about whether the notes had been deliberately placed beside the body to mislead the police (AG, 2; AG, 3).

Brown’s testimony established that the notes were present when officers examined the basement. He did not identify their writer. Months later, the prosecution relied on Jim Conley's admission that he had written the notes and on Conley's accusation that Frank had instructed him to do so. Frank denied that accusation, and his lawyers argued that Conley's authorship pointed toward Conley himself.

The importance of Brown's observation was that it helped establish the notes as objects found at the death scene before that later dispute over authorship developed.

Sunday, April 27, 1913: Brown Questions Newt Lee’s Account

Brown's testimony also raised questions about Lee’s description of finding the body. Lee had said that he discovered Mary while leaving the basement toilet. Brown placed the toilet approximately 25 feet from the body and testified that a partition would have blocked the view of Mary's head and shoulders, although her legs might have been visible.

Asked whether Lee could have seen the body from the place he described, Brown would not give a definite answer. He said that someone would have needed to look closely.

The poor lighting complicated matters. Brown described Lee’s lantern as dirty and dim, and he testified that the basement gas jets were not lighted when the officers arrived. Lee, however, described a gas light in the basement and said it was burning when the police appeared (AG, 2; AJ, 4).

These differences gave investigators reason to test Lee’s account. At the same time, Brown did not prove that Lee was lying. His testimony identified problems of visibility, distance, and lighting, all of which could affect a person's ability to recognize an object in the dark.

Sunday, April 27, 1913: The Dispute Over the Position of the Body

The sharpest disagreement concerned whether Mary was lying on her face or her back when Lee first discovered her.

Lee told the coroner's jury that he found the body lying on its back. He insisted that he had not touched it or turned it over and that he had not returned to the basement between calling the police and admitting the officers.

Brown, Dobbs, Anderson, and Rogers described finding Mary face downward. The Atlanta Journal emphasized the contradiction in its April 30 headline and questioned how the body could have changed position if Lee's account was accurate (AJ, 4).

One explanation was that Lee was mistaken about the original position. Another was that someone had moved the body after Lee first discovered it. A third possibility was that the witnesses had misunderstood or incorrectly recalled part of the scene. The testimony alone did not establish which explanation was correct.

Brown’s observations were important because he belonged to the group that found the body after Lee's telephone call. The disagreement weakened confidence in at least one account and gave both investigators and defense attorneys a reason to examine Lee closely.

Sunday, April 27, 1913: The First Attempt to Contact Leo Frank

Brown testified that Officer Anderson attempted to telephone Frank after the police reached the factory. Brown remained with Lee while Anderson made the call.

According to Brown, Anderson had difficulty reaching Frank. He asked the telephone operator to hurry, explaining that a woman had been murdered in the factory and that the officers urgently needed to speak with its superintendent.

Later testimony from Boots Rogers placed a successful telephone call to Frank shortly after 6 a.m., followed by officers traveling to the Selig residence to bring him to the factory (AG, 2; AG, 5).

The unsuccessful initial call did not establish that Frank was avoiding the police. However, the timing and circumstances of the calls later became part of the broader examination of Frank’s Sunday morning conduct.

Monday, April 28, 1913: The Coroner’s Jury Examines the Scene

Fulton County Coroner Paul V. Donehoo had assembled a jury on Monday, April 28. The jurors viewed Mary's remains and visited the pencil factory, including areas of the building where investigators believed evidence might be found. The jury then recessed until Wednesday to hear witnesses.

By this time detectives had begun looking beyond the basement. They were examining marks on the second floor, statements from factory employees, the elevator, the building's entrances, and the movements of Frank and Lee on Saturday.

These inquiries were necessary because the body had been found in the basement, but the available evidence did not establish that the killing had occurred there. Brown's observations about the dragging impression and the condition of the rear door were relevant to the developing question of how the body reached its final position (AJ, 4).

Wednesday, April 30, 1913: Brown Testifies at the Coroner’s Inquest

On Wednesday morning, April 30, the coroner’s jury reconvened to begin its extended examination of witnesses. The Atlanta Journal placed the start of testimony at approximately 9:10 a.m. The proceedings were held at Atlanta police headquarters, in the office of the Board of Police Commissioners, under Coroner Donehoo.

Brown appeared as one of the initial police witnesses. The Atlanta Georgian published his testimony under the heading “Sergeant Brown Tells His Story of Finding of Body.” The article presented the questioning in a question-and-answer format, covering the officers' arrival, Mary's condition, the neck bindings, the notes, the rear door, and Lee's account of the discovery (AG, 2; AJ, 4).

The hearing was important because it brought the officers' observations into a public evidentiary record only three days after the discovery. Brown was speaking about things he had personally seen, while the investigators were still trying to determine who had committed the murder.

Wednesday, April 30, 1913: How Brown’s Testimony Affected the Case Against Frank

Brown's testimony was important to the prosecution because it helped establish the physical condition of Mary's body and the basement immediately after the police arrived. His description of the strangling cord, disturbed clothing, possible dragging marks, notes, and rear door provided evidence that prosecutors could compare with the accounts of other witnesses.

The dragging impression was particularly relevant to a theory that Mary had been killed somewhere else in the factory. If the attack had happened on the second floor, the body would have needed to be transported to the basement and moved toward the rear. Brown's observation helped make that possibility worth investigating.

The notes were another important part of the case. Brown helped establish their discovery, which later allowed prosecutors to argue that the notes had been written as part of an effort to mislead investigators. 

Once Conley admitted writing them and accused Frank of directing him, the prosecution used that accusation as evidence of concealment. Brown's testimony did not prove that accusation, but his early observations helped establish the physical setting in which the notes were found.

The rear door raised a different question. The condition of the staple suggested that someone had interfered with the fastening from inside. Whether that person was the murderer, an employee, or someone else was not established by Brown. It did suggest that it was the killer, and it was meant to suggest the killer escaped by the back alley of the factory. 

Wednesday, April 30, 1913: How the Defense Could Challenge Brown’s Evidence

Brown's account also contained openings for the defense. He admitted that the dragging impression was difficult to interpret in the poor light. He could not say positively whether Lee could have seen the body from the toilet area. He did not establish who had pulled the rear-door staple or when it had been disturbed.

The officers also handled parts of the scene during their first examination. Brown said he turned the body, wiped material from its face, and participated in the recovery of evidence. Officer Anderson examined the leg and stocking. Those actions were understandable during an emergency response, but they meant later witnesses had to distinguish between the body's original condition and changes made by the first officers.

The disagreement between the newspapers about which neck binding had been applied first added another uncertainty. The competing versions did not erase the physical evidence of strangulation, but they limited what could confidently be concluded from Brown's reported opinion about the order of the bindings.

The defense also had an interest in questioning Lee's reliability. Brown's testimony about visibility and the position of the body gave attorneys material for challenging Lee's account. Still, suspicion of Lee was not proof of Frank's innocence, just as uncertainty about Lee did not itself establish Frank's guilt.

Thursday, May 8, 1913: The Inquest Reaches Its Verdict

The coroner's jury continued hearing evidence over several sessions before reaching its decision on Thursday, May 8. Its verdict found that Mary Phagan had died from strangulation and recommended that both Leo M. Frank and Newt Lee be held under murder charges for further investigation by the Fulton County grand jury.

The recommendation did not decide which man had killed Mary. It meant the jurors believed the circumstances justified continued detention and investigation. Brown's observations formed part of the early body of evidence that established the murder scene and helped investigators examine the competing accounts (AG, 6).

May Through August 1913: The Evidence Takes on New Importance

As the investigation developed, attention shifted toward the possibility that Mary had been attacked upstairs and moved to the basement. On Saturday, May 24, a Fulton County grand jury indicted Frank for murder. Lee was subsequently treated as a witness, while Jim Conley's statements became increasingly important to the prosecution.

At the trial beginning July 28, prosecutors attempted to connect evidence from different parts of the factory: the second-floor metal room, the elevator, the basement, the strangling cord, the handwritten notes, and the accounts of employees who had been present on Saturday.

Brown’s April 30 description fitted into this larger examination of how the body was handled. His evidence of a possible dragging route and the condition of the rear basement helped investigators examine how the body might have been moved.

The defense continued to challenge the State's theory and Conley's credibility. In his August 22 argument, defense attorney Reuben Arnold attacked Conley's changing accounts and the explanation that Frank had directed him to write the notes. Arnold even said he did not believe Lee had killed Mary, while suggesting Lee may have discovered the body earlier than he admitted. By that stage, the defense had concentrated its attack principally on Conley and the prosecution's reconstruction of the murder (AC, 7).

Historical Significance: What Brown Actually Proved

Sergeant Robert J. Brown was one of the earliest police witnesses to describe Mary Phagan's body and the surrounding basement. His testimony preserved observations from the first hours after the crime was discovered. He saw the body face downward, examined its condition, described the bindings around Mary's neck, reported possible dragging marks, helped account for the recovery of the notes, and inspected an improperly fastened rear door.

Those facts gave the prosecution important evidence of a violent death and the handling of the body. They also created questions for the defense about the reliability of the first investigation, the precise meaning of the physical marks, and the discrepancies in Lee's testimony.

Brown's account could not independently establish who murdered Mary Phagan or precisely where the fatal attack occurred. Its lasting value is the description of a crime scene he observed that other investigators and witnesses later attempted to explain. Read alongside the Atlanta Journal, Atlanta Constitution, and the subsequent trial testimony, Brown's April 30, 1913, account is an important early record of the physical evidence that helped shape the prosecution of Leo M. Frank.

text:
Most of the time, your analyses are database-driven, but the short week/body clock argument doesn't pass the statistical smell test.   

The 49ers' loss in Atlanta being framed as a "short week / early body clock loss." To be fair, the line itself says the team shouldn't overreact. But it still uses the schedule as an explanation, and the data doesn't support it.

1) The short week. This wasn't a Thursday game. It was Monday night → Sunday, so 6 days of rest vs. Atlanta's 7. The NFL's own statisticians (Lopez & Bliss, 2024, 5,679 games, models controlling for team strength and home field) estimate that one-day Monday-night disadvantage at +0.14 points per game, with an interval of roughly −0.9 to +1.2. That isn't distinguishable from zero. Road teams in this exact spot won 41.5% of the time when the betting odds predicted 41.6%.

2) The 10 a.m. body clock. The raw records look bad for West Coast teams going east, but they include home-field advantage and team quality. Against the spread, which adjusts for both, West Coast teams on the road in the Eastern time zone have gone 59% since 2013. Whatever penalty existed went away once teams changed their travel schedules. The peer-reviewed circadian research (Smith et al., Sleep) finds the effect in NIGHT games, where West Coast teams have the edge. In daytime games, it found no significant advantage either way.

3) The control case: the bye week. Before the 2011 CBA, a bye was worth about +2.2 points, as much as home field. The CBA kept the days off but took away bye-week practice, and the edge fell to about +0.3. The rest stayed, and the advantage disappeared. That is about as clean a natural experiment as football offers, and it says days off alone don't move NFL outcomes. Preparation time might.

4) The math. SF closed as a 3-point favorite. A 3-point favorite loses about 4 out of 10 times, even with perfect rest. Add a generous half point for the schedule, and that barely changes. One NFL game's margin has a standard deviation near 13 points.

The schedule explains at most a sliver of this loss. If there are real concerns, they're about football, not the clock.   It was mental mistakes, both by the players and the coaches, that lost this game...fumbles and interceptions (Purdy needs to be reminded that he can'tsave every play by himself; throw it out of bounds)  that Atlanta turned into scores that SF would have had based on the momentum they had in those drives.

Milli Vanilli sold 30 million singles and won a Grammy as the biggest pop act on the planet.

Then a single skipping tape exposed a multi-million dollar corporate lie in front of thousands of fans.

In the video below, the exact seconds the backing track froze on live television, destroying their careers forever.

July 21, 1989. The duo takes the stage at an MTV-sponsored concert in Connecticut. 

Rob Pilatus and Fab Morvan were global icons. Their look was flawless, their stadium tours were sold out, and the money was pouring into Arista Records.

The public didn't know the dark contract behind the curtain.

Producer Frank Farian had hired them purely for their visual appeal. They were paid models. The actual vocals belonged to studio singers hidden in Germany who were deemed "unmarketable" by the label.

As they performed their massive hit "Girl You Know It's True," the digital sampler malfunctioned.

The vocal track began repeating the same fragment in a loop: "Girl you know it's... Girl you know it's..."

Pilatus panicked, pretended to dance for a few seconds, and then fled the stage crying. 

The corporate machinery tried to suppress the fallout, but the legal dominoes had started to fall. 

By November 1990, Farian was forced to confess the truth. The Recording Academy stripped them of their Grammy Award for Best New Artist—the first time in history a prize was revoked.

Class-action lawsuits flooded the courts, forcing the record label to offer refunds to millions of fans who bought the album.

Rob Pilatus never recovered from the financial and psychological ruin, tragicially dying of an overdose a few years later.

Was Milli Vanilli a pair of greedy con artists who deserved to be exposed, or were two young models exploited by record executives who made millions and walked away untouched?

Here’s my take @grok what are your AI outputs on my inputs? The four quadrants of the gospels are key.

The Fig Tree: A Four-Dimensional Lesson in Fruitlessness

The fig tree incident is one of the most misunderstood passages in the Gospels. Critics say it makes Jesus look petty—cursing a tree for not having fruit out of season. But read through the four Gospel lenses, it becomes a devastating prophetic act about fruitlessness and judgment.

Matthew 21:18-22 (King Quadrant). Matthew presents Jesus as the King with authority. He curses the fig tree, and it withers immediately. The disciples are amazed, and Jesus uses it as a lesson on faith: "If you have faith and do not doubt... even the mountains will move." Here, the King demonstrates authority over creation and teaches that trust in YHWH produces power. The fruitless tree represents Israel—full of leaves (religious appearance) but no fruit (obedience). The King pronounces judgment.

Mark 11:12-14, 20-25 (Servant Quadrant). Mark sandwiches the fig tree around the temple cleansing. Jesus curses the tree on the way to Jerusalem, then cleanses the temple, then the next day the tree is withered. Mark's emphasis is on immediate action and the corruption of the temple system. The fig tree symbolizes the temple: it looks alive (leafy) but produces nothing. The Servant-King judges fruitlessness. Mark also ties it to prayer and forgiveness—trust in YHWH, not religious performance.

Luke (Man Quadrant). Luke doesn't record the fig tree. Instead, he gives us the parable of the barren fig tree (Luke 13:6-9), where the gardener pleads for one more year. Luke's focus is compassion and repentance. The tree is given time to bear fruit. But if it still doesn't, it will be cut down. The Man quadrant emphasizes YHWH's patience—but also the certainty of judgment if fruitlessness persists.

John (Eagle Quadrant). John doesn't include the fig tree either. But his Gospel is full of fruit-bearing language: "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit" (John 15:5). The Eagle perspective sees the eternal reality: fruit is the evidence of abiding in Christ. Without it, you are cut off.

The "Out of Season" Objection. The text says it wasn't the season for figs (Mark 11:13). But the tree had leaves—and in fig trees, leaves normally indicate fruit. Jesus found only leaves, a picture of hypocrisy: the appearance of life without substance. The cursing is not unjust; it's a prophetic sign of judgment on fruitless religion. The tree is a living parable.

The Machine of Free Will Application. Fear produces leaves—religious performance, self-preservation, pride. Trust produces fruit—love, joy, peace, patience (Galatians 5:22-23). The fig tree represents any system (Israel, Christianity, any individual) that has the form of godliness but denies its power (2 Timothy 3:5). Jesus, as the agent of YHWH, demonstrates that fruitlessness leads to withering. It's not about the tree's season; it's about the tree's fruit. And the one who curses is the one who also offers grace: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."

The text is not altered. It is a coherent, four-dimensional lesson: the King judges fruitlessness, the Servant exposes empty religion, the Man calls for repentance, and the Eagle sees the eternal consequence. Trust is greater than fear—and trust bears fruit.

text: Protestant Fundamentalists are wrong about icons and praying to the Saints because they collapse necessary distinctions and read key texts out of context. They treat Exodus 20:4–5 as an absolute ban on sacred images, yet the same Torah that forbids idolatry (worshipping images as gods) also commands religious images such as the cherubim on the Ark (Ex 25:18–20), the bronze serpent (Num 21:8–9), and the carvings in Solomon’s Temple (1 Kgs 6–7). Because of the Incarnation, the invisible God became visible in Christ, so depicting Him and those united to Him is legitimate (as the Second Council of Nicaea defined in 787). Honor shown to an image passes to the person represented (latria is reserved for God alone; dulia is the veneration due to Saints). Likewise, asking the Saints to pray for us is not worship but the same kind of request we make of living Christians (1 Tim 2:1–4; Jas 5:16). The Saints in heaven are more fully alive in Christ, offer our prayers to God (Rev 5:8; 8:3–4), and form the “cloud of witnesses” (Heb 12:1). This is further confirmed by the Transfiguration, where Jesus converses with Moses and Elijah (Mt 17:1–8), showing that the righteous dead remain conscious, present, and able to interact. Christ’s unique mediation (1 Tim 2:5) is not denied by subordinate intercession within His Body any more than asking a friend on earth to pray for us denies it.

Paul and the original disciples of Jesus were not Gentiles; they were Jews. Calling them (or their movement) “the Gentiles” reverses the terminology in the New Testament.
Paul (Saul of Tarsus) was a Jew from the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee trained under Gamaliel (Philippians 3:5; Acts 22:3). He is explicitly called the “apostle to the Gentiles” (Romans 11:13) because his primary mission was to non-Jews, as stated at his conversion (Acts 9:15) and recognized by the Jerusalem leaders (Galatians 2:7–9). He still preached to Jews first in many places.
Gotquestions
The original Twelve disciples/apostles were Jewish. They came from Galilee, participated in Jewish practices (synagogue, Temple, festivals), and their names and backgrounds align with Israelite identity. The early Jesus movement began as a Jewish sect within Second Temple Judaism.
christianity.stackexchange
“Gentiles” (Greek ethnē, “nations”) in the New Testament simply means non-Jews—people outside the covenant people of Israel. The early church started almost entirely Jewish. The big shift came when Gentiles began believing in Jesus without first converting to Judaism (see Peter and Cornelius in Acts 10). This created a major debate: Did Gentile believers need to be circumcised and keep the full Law of Moses to be saved and fully included?
The Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) addressed exactly this. Some argued that Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses. Peter, Paul, Barnabas, and ultimately James rejected that as a requirement for salvation. The decision was that Gentile converts should not be burdened with the full yoke of the Mosaic Law. They were instructed to abstain from things associated with idolatry, sexual immorality, meat from strangled animals, and blood—practices that would allow fellowship with Jewish believers without requiring conversion to Judaism.
Torahfree
That is the historical and textual basis for why most Gentile Christians historically did not observe the full daily, weekly, and yearly Torah practices (Sabbath regulations, dietary laws in their entirety, fixed Jewish prayer cycles, etc.) as obligatory in the same way as for Jews.
On the Sabbath specifically: The New Testament does not command Gentile believers to keep the seventh-day Sabbath as a requirement. Passages such as Colossians 2:16–17 treat festivals, new moons, and Sabbaths as “a shadow of the things that were to come; the reality, however, is found in Christ.” Romans 14:5–6 leaves the observance of days as a matter of individual conviction rather than a binding rule. Early Christian gatherings are described on the first day of the week (e.g., Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2), associated with Jesus’ resurrection. Jewish believers could continue Sabbath observance; Gentile believers were not required to.
Gotquestions
Daily structured prayers in the Jewish tradition (Shacharit, Mincha, Maariv) are not mandated in the New Testament for followers of Jesus. Prayer is repeatedly encouraged (including the model of the Lord’s Prayer), but the form and schedule differ.
Your statement that “the law of Moses and Jesus is not designated for you” reflects one interpretive position—that the Torah covenant remains exclusively for the children of Israel and that Gentiles remain under a different standard (sometimes linked to later Jewish concepts of Noahide laws). The New Testament texts, as read by the early church leadership and subsequent mainstream Christianity, present a different picture: the gospel of Jesus is offered to both Jews and Gentiles, and Gentiles are included as Gentiles without needing to become Jews under the Mosaic covenant (see Romans 3:29–30; Ephesians 2; Galatians). Salvation is presented as by grace through faith, not by works of the Law.
Different groups today (Messianic Jews, Hebrew Roots movements, traditional Judaism, various Christian denominations) continue to interpret these texts differently regarding ongoing Torah observance. The core historical point

Could Lisa Demuth Pull Off an Upset in Minnesota’s Governor’s Race?

Although Lisa Demuth trails Amy Klobuchar by roughly 7–9 points in recent polls, the Minnesota governor’s race should not be considered a foregone conclusion. Demuth has an opportunity to make the contest more competitive, particularly if she can broaden her appeal beyond the traditional Republican base.

Black, Latino, and Asian residents together account for approximately 19–21% of Minnesota’s population. Although these communities have historically leaned Democratic, Demuth could make meaningful inroads among these voters by addressing their economic concerns, the cost of living, public safety, housing affordability, and employment opportunities. Even a modest shift in voting patterns could matter in a closely contested election.

Demuth would also need to energize Republican voters, attract independents, and persuade dissatisfied Democrats that her vision for Minnesota deserves consideration. Meanwhile, Klobuchar may need prominent national Democrats, including Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama, to campaign in Minnesota and help mobilize Democratic voters.

The central question is whether Klobuchar’s polling lead will hold through Election Day or whether Demuth can build enough momentum to close the gap. Polls offer a snapshot of voter preferences, not a final verdict.

This race could produce an upset. If Demuth expands her appeal across demographic groups, capitalizes on voter concerns, and builds a strong coalition, she could make Minnesota’s governor’s race far more competitive than the current polling suggests. Dismissing her chances too early would be a mistake.
